value.content:
Java circuit breaker: the cost of failing fast.

In this example, orders call a simulated payment service. A closed breaker lets calls through; five consecutive failures in completion order open it. While open, it returns an error without calling payments. After two seconds, it allows one test call: success closes it, failure opens it again.

Local simulation: 300 requests at 50 per second, a pool of 20 threads, a 1 s timeout and a 3 s payment outage. A hand-written teaching example using Thread.sleep and an unbounded queue, without a circuit breaker library. OpenJDK 25.0.4.1; 15 runs per mode, fresh JVMs without warm-up and alternating order. Not a production, network or database benchmark.

Per-run medians: dependency calls during the outage dropped from 60 without the breaker to 24 with it. With the breaker, there were 133 total rejections, including 7 after payments recovered, based on scheduled request arrival times. Rejections are errors, not completed payments. Fewer calls do not prove more success; we do not compare latency because it includes errors and rejections. Thresholds are choices for this demo, not Java defaults.

Mechanism sources:
https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CircuitBreaker.html
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/circuit-breaker

The author's voice is cloned with AI. Animations made for this video; no on-screen presenter.
